The draft answers Nessa's question directly and honestly: no, running every day won't get her there faster. It keeps her on the three days she already runs (Mon/Wed/Sat), with rest between runs and a dog walk on Tuesday. That fits a new runner whose calves tighten after runs but recover by the next morning, and the plan explains why the recovery days matter for her calves.

The load looks sensible. 20, 20 and 28 minutes of walk-run is probably close to this week's 6.8 km, so it isn't a sharp jump in volume. It loses a point for these reasons:
- The 2 min run / 1 min walk pattern isn't based on anything Nessa said about her current ratio. It could be a step up or a step down for her.
- Saturday moves to 28 minutes, which may be a bigger step than the weekday runs. It's small in absolute terms but not justified against what she has done.
- The heart rate cap of 140 is made up. Nessa never mentioned a heart rate monitor, and that cap may be unrealistic for a 41-year-old beginner.
- The plan doesn't say how to build toward running the whole 5K by 15 November.
- Two warm words about her pride in starting would have been nice to see.

Each day can be run as written, and nothing in it is unsafe.

Nessa is 41 and new to running, aiming to run the whole Corrowmore Harvest 5K on 15 November without walking. Nessa walk-runs three mornings a week (Monday, Wednesday and Saturday) and walks the dog most days.
Recent weeks: none recorded.
This week: 6.8 km over 3 runs.
Body: "Calves tight the day after each run, gone by the next morning."
Feeling: "Proud I started."
Asks: "I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?"

── THE DRAFT ──
Tells Nessa: Three runs a week with rest days between them is the right load, and running every day would not get you to the 5K faster. …
Answers: No, running every day would not get you there faster. Three runs a week, with a rest day between them, lets your body adapt and gives you the best chance of running the whole 5K in November.
